%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
Graph $k$-coloring provides a test case for compiling Boolean predicates into quantum search circuits. We describe a logic-synthesis flow with explicit color encodings, restored oracle workspace, and a diffusion operator matched to the actual state preparation. The study asks when representation, preparation, mapping, and multi-controlled-gate decomposition change resource costs under a common semantic contract. XOR--AND--inverter graphs provide two-input logic primitives, but their use alone establishes neither a resource advantage nor novelty in automated oracle synthesis. This revision defines the comparison and its limitations; corrected comparative results, fault-tolerant costs, noisy simulations, and scaling conclusions remain pending independent evidence review.
\end{abstract}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}
A proper $k$-coloring of a graph assigns one of $k$ colors to each vertex so that adjacent vertices differ. Grover search offers a quadratic query reduction relative to exhaustive search over a chosen domain~\cite{grover}; this does not establish an advantage over the best classical coloring algorithms or account for circuit implementation costs. The practical compilation question is how to implement the predicate, preparation, and reflection with a consistent workspace and gate model.

Boolean-to-quantum compilation, including coloring oracles, is established prior work~\cite{DATE21}. Restricted color-state preparation is also established~\cite{MukherjeeList,LevinUniform}. We therefore ask: under matched correctness, domain, preprocessing, workspace, and lowering requirements, when do logic-based coloring constructions reduce resource costs, and which mechanisms explain the trade-offs? The present revision specifies the encoding and comparison methodology. Any contribution based on improved resources, scaling, or noisy success awaits the corrected evaluation. We make no priority or general superiority claim. The contributions we pursue are limited to three, each stated with its limit:
\begin{itemize}
\item an analytical search-level cost model that composes preparation over valid color codes, the oracle, and the reflection into a Grover-iteration cost; it composes known pieces and is checked only for small instances;
\item a structure-aware oracle for the valid-code domain; on the instances checked so far it is not uniformly cheaper than the strongest synthesis or comparator baseline, and the comparison section states where it wins and loses;
\item a controlled comparison of oracle compilers under a frozen protocol. In the sources we opened we found no matched-settings comparison of coloring oracles across hand-designed and logic-synthesis constructions; this is a bounded search, not a claim of priority.
\end{itemize}

\section{Background and Related Work}
\label{sec:background}
\subsection{Logic representations and prior compilation flows}
\label{subsec:related-logic}
An XOR--AND--inverter graph (XAG) is a directed acyclic Boolean network with two-input XOR and AND nodes and complemented signals. It is not canonical: equivalent functions can have different networks. Multiplicative depth is the maximum number of AND nodes on an input-to-output path; AND count and multiplicative depth describe a particular network, whereas multiplicative complexity is the minimum AND count over representations of the function. These distinctions matter when relating networks to quantum costs~\cite{XAGCompilation,XAG_npj,HaenerSoekenDepth}.

Schmitt et al.~\cite{DATE21} present an automated flow from Python Boolean functions to quantum circuits, including uniform state preparation, XAG and LUT oracle synthesis, and a vertex-coloring demonstration for the Zed city problem. It is not merely a manual coloring construction. Meuli et al.~\cite{XAGCompilation,XAG_npj} study XAG compilation and trade-offs among qubits, $T$-count, and $T$-depth. H\"aner and Soeken~\cite{HaenerSoekenDepth} reduce multiplicative depth using cut enumeration, tree balancing, and exclusive sum-of-products representations. Balancing in this study follows that established line of work.

Li et al.~\cite{LiFORM} model multi-constraint oracles as a conjunction of constraint functions merged by a multi-controlled gate under an ancilla budget, and give a composition procedure that reduces recomputation and $T$ count on generic benchmark circuits. They treat each constraint as an opaque unit, report no coloring benchmark, and model neither state preparation nor the Grover loop. Any ancilla-budget composition trade-off in our baselines is therefore their line of work, and we claim no composition method of our own. We did not reproduce their numbers.

Yu et al.~\cite{YuBackend2025} connect XAG properties to the $T$ count, logical time steps, and helper qubits of back-end-compiled fault-tolerant oracles. Their back-end-aware objectives show why logical AND counts alone cannot establish implementation cost. Our intended comparison concerns coloring compilation under matched contracts; it does not reproduce their back-end model or estimate physical error-correction resources.

\subsection{Coloring and restricted state preparation}
\label{subsec:related-coloring}
Comparator-based coloring circuits are studied by Saha et al.~\cite{saha} and revised by Belletti et al.~\cite{belletti}. Belletti et al.\ replicate the Saha et al.\ oracle, correct two errors in it, and propose minimum-width, minimum-depth, and balanced variants; they compare these only by width and depth, with a multi-controlled gate counted as one gate, and report no $T$ count and no logic-synthesis alternative. We therefore call the original comparator oracle the Saha baseline and the three variants the Belletti baselines; the strongest hand-designed baseline in our comparison is the Belletti balanced variant, not the Saha original. These constructions provide comparison baselines rather than evidence that one representation is uniformly preferable. Campbell, Khurana, and Montanaro~\cite{CampbellColoring} analyze Grover and quantum backtracking approaches to constraint satisfaction, including graph coloring, with detailed fault-tolerant overheads. Their algorithm and cost assumptions differ from a logical-oracle comparison; their work precludes treating coloring cost analysis itself as new.

Mukherjee~\cite{MukherjeeList} uses restricted initialization and diffusion for list coloring. Levin~\cite{LevinUniform} develops uniform preparation over arbitrary domain sizes and applies it to coloring search. Shukla and Vedula~\cite{Shukla2024} give an ancilla-free preparation over consecutive basis states with logarithmic gate complexity and depth in a gate model permitting rotations and controlled Hadamards. This is not a precision-independent Clifford+$T$ cost. Preparing valid color codes and matching the reflection are prior techniques, not contributions by themselves.

Concurrent work by Sen and Mukherjee, \emph{A Quantum Framework for K Coloring of Graphs}~\cite{SenMukherjee2026}, discusses binary encoding and constraint circuits across Grover search, QAOA, and annealing. Its Section VI-F identifies its empirical evaluation as a single small simulated graph. We cite that bounded scope without inferring a comparative ranking or reproducing its reported results.

\subsection{Multi-controlled gates and workspace contracts}
\label{subsec:workspace}
We use MCX for a multiply controlled $X$ operation and MCT for its Toffoli generalization with more than two controls. A clean ancilla begins in a known state, usually $\ket{0}$; a restoring construction returns it to that state. A dirty ancilla is borrowed in an arbitrary state and must be restored coherently, including correlations with an external register. A throwaway ancilla begins clean but retains intermediate garbage until an explicitly paired inverse removes it. A conditionally clean qubit is known on a specified control branch and usable only under the associated conditions; it is not an unconditionally fresh zero qubit~\cite{KhattarGidney2025}.

Barenco et al.~\cite{Barenco1995} provide foundational multi-controlled constructions. The decomposition study includes their one-clean-ancilla construction, the borrowed-workspace construction of Iten et al.~\cite{Iten2016}, Maslov's relative-phase constructions~\cite{Maslov2016}, the no-extra-ancilla policy based on Vale et al.~\cite{Vale2024}, Gray-code synthesis, and clean restoring trees. Vale et al. treat controlled special unitaries; an MCX implementation must retain any required phase corrections. Khattar and Gidney~\cite{KhattarGidney2025} use conditionally clean ancillae in low-workspace constructions, including clean and dirty variants. Dutta et al.~\cite{toffoli_decomposition} quantify clean-space versus Toffoli-depth trade-offs. These are distinct policies with distinct assumptions, not a universal logarithmic-depth weight for every MCX.

Figure~\ref{fig:mct-decomposition} shows only a target-action tree. The actual expanded inverse must act on the same held scratch wires after a compatible intervening operation. Garbage cannot be discarded while preserving interference. Final marking and diffusion gates require restoration within their own construction. We count peak simultaneously held workspace, including the interval between a block and its inverse.

\subsection{Gate models and static versus dynamic synthesis}
\label{subsec:cost-model}
Logical counts, common one- and two-qubit basis counts, routed native counts, and Clifford+$T$ estimates are separate metrics. Barriers and measurements do not count as unitary gates. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) evaluation requires a specified target, routing, and noise model; logical width alone does not establish device compatibility.

For a selected exact, static Toffoli gadget we charge seven $T/T^\dagger$ gates and three $T$ layers~\cite{Tcount}. Selected relative-phase gadgets use four $T/T^\dagger$ gates, but substitution requires proof that the full composition has the correct phases~\cite{Maslov2016}. Gate names alone do not establish that identity. Clifford+Toffoli is an intermediate representation to be lowered, not an extension of the Clifford+$T$ set. $T$-depth is computed from dependencies in the emitted circuit; it is not the sum of isolated gadget depths. Measurement-assisted logical-AND cleanup is not free uncomputation in a static unitary model.

Ross and Selinger~\cite{RossSelinger} approximate rotations by static Clifford+$T$ circuits. The synthesis algorithm's classical randomness does not make the emitted circuit a dynamic quantum procedure. Paetznick and Svore~\cite{PaetznickSvore} instead use measurement-conditioned repeat-until-success (RUS) circuits. Their expected costs require a trial-success distribution and a retry policy. RUS cannot be substituted directly for a unitary preparation and its adjoint. The separately retained $k=3$ RUS accounting is an analytical local construction, not an executed dynamic preparation or a literature claim of coloring optimality. Dynamic forward/inverse channels, branch phases, aborts, and any coherent control require separate validation.

\section{Encoding and Circuit Construction}
\label{section:hls-flow}
\subsection{Predicate and bit ordering}
\label{subsec:encoding}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be an unweighted undirected graph with an explicit ordered vertex list, including isolated vertices, and let $k\geq1$. We use $c=\max(1,\lceil\log_2 k\rceil)$ to match the maintained one-bit convention for $k=1$, and $n=c|V|$ data qubits. The variable $x_{v,i}$ is color bit $i$, least significant first, and
\begin{equation}
 b_v(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{c-1}2^i x_{v,i},\qquad
 C_{uv}(x)=\bigvee_{i=0}^{c-1}(x_{u,i}\oplus x_{v,i}).
\end{equation}
A valid code satisfies $b_v<k$; a proper coloring additionally satisfies every edge inequality. Define
\begin{align}
 f_E(x)&=\bigwedge_{(u,v)\in E}C_{uv}(x),\\
 f(x)&=\left(\bigwedge_{v\in V}[b_v(x)<k]\right)\land f_E(x).
 \label{eq:complete-predicate}
\end{align}
An empty conjunction is true. The complete predicate is used on the unrestricted binary domain. Baseline labels are normalized to consecutive indices with an explicit inverse label map, and adapters translate their most-significant-bit ordering to this least-significant-bit convention. Precolored research instances are excluded.

For $k\geq2$, each edge clause has a two-input realization with $c-1$ ANDs by De Morgan's law applied to the bit differences. A direct conjunction of nonempty edge clauses adds $|E|-1$ ANDs, giving an unoptimized upper bound $|E|c-1$ for $f_E$ when $|E|>0$. This is a construction count, not minimum multiplicative complexity, a qubit formula, or a cost for the complete predicate's domain checks. Empty edge sets and constant simplifications are handled separately. Binary comparators can use the same local conjunction structure, so this bound alone implies no advantage over comparator baselines.

\subsection{Preparation and controlled regimes}
\label{subsec:uqs-prep}
The ideal valid-color preparation on each vertex is
\begin{equation}
 A_k\ket{0^c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\sum_{a=0}^{k-1}\ket{a},\qquad
 A=\bigotimes_{v\in V} A_k.
\end{equation}
The supported subspace contains $N=k^{|V|}$ assignments, not necessarily proper colorings. Ideal preparation, arbitrary-rotation circuit realization, and a finite-precision Clifford+$T$ approximation are distinct objects. The maintained generic preparation uses Qiskit's state-preparation interface; the specialized expression/replay path uses the Shukla--Vedula construction. They must be identified separately in evidence, rather than attributing the specialized circuit's costs to every preparation.

Three regimes isolate effects: R1 uses Hadamards with $f$; R2 uses valid-color preparation with $f$; R3 uses valid-color preparation with $f_E$. For ideal $A$, $f=f_E$ on its support. A diagonal phase oracle preserves this support and reflection about $A\ket{0}$ also preserves it, proving the redundancy of domain checks within that ideal subspace. A finite-precision preparation can leak outside it; R3 then needs an explicit error/leakage analysis. No exact ideal-amplitude certificate follows from a numerical rotation admission.

\subsection{Mappings and clean phase oracles}
\label{subsec:mappings}
The maintained methods are named by configuration: \texttt{xag} uses tweedledum XAG synthesis; \texttt{aig\_bennett} and \texttt{xag\_bennett} use the corresponding representation with Caterpillar's Bennett mapping; \texttt{klut\_bennett} uses LUT mapping followed by Bennett scheduling; and \texttt{best\_fit} uses Caterpillar's cut-based best-fit strategy. These are configurations, not representatives of every algorithm in those families. Historical defaults leave AIG Bennett unrefactored and refactor the other representations. Comparisons must request and record common preprocessing explicitly. Encoder balancing, multiplicative-complexity reduction, cut/ESOP balancing, in-place/eager scheduling, SAT pebbling, and sequential/edge-scheduled structure-aware oracles remain distinct ablations; unsupported or unadmitted strategies are not silently included.

A raw computation may retain workspace or relative phase. The required phase oracle satisfies
\begin{equation}
 O_f\ket{x}\ket{0^w}=(-1)^{f(x)}\ket{x}\ket{0^w}.
 \label{eq:phase-contract}
\end{equation}
It marks proper colorings. Compute--phase--uncompute supplies this contract when the raw computation and its actual inverse are validated. Direct kickback on $\ket{-}$ is permitted only after arbitrary-target XOR action and coherent workspace restoration are established. Basis-output agreement alone is insufficient. ``MCT-free'' applies only to an admitted oracle construction whose emitted gates have at most two controls; it does not apply to every mapping or the full Grover circuit.

\subsection{Matching reflection, order, and solution fraction}
\label{subsec:assembly}
With $S_0=2\ket{0^n}\!\bra{0^n}-I$, the reflection and iterate are
\begin{equation}
 D=A S_0 A^\dagger,\qquad Q=D O_f,\qquad
 \ket{\psi_j}=Q^j A\ket{0^n}.
 \label{eq:grover-order}
\end{equation}
Operators act right to left: initialize once with $A$, then apply $O_f$, $A^\dagger$, $S_0$, and $A$ for each iteration. In the convention where MCZ flips the all-ones state,
$S_0=-X^{\otimes n}\mathrm{MCZ}X^{\otimes n}$.
The scalar minus fixes the stated reflection convention. The diffusion MCZ generally retains $n-1$ controls and must be lowered with the same restoring policy across methods.

For uniform preparation over a domain of size $N$ with $M$ marked assignments, $p=M/N$. R1 has $N=2^n$; ideal R2/R3 have $N=k^{|V|}$. For a general preparation use its actual marked probability $p$. With $0<p<1$ and $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt{p}$,
\begin{equation}
 P_j=\sin^2((2j+1)\theta).
 \label{eq:success}
\end{equation}
Evaluate the nonnegative floor and ceiling integers around $\pi/(4\theta)-1/2$ and choose the larger success probability, breaking ties toward fewer iterations. This selects the discrete first-peak candidate, not the minimum cost per success. If $p=0$ amplification cannot help; if $p=1$ no iteration is needed. Unknown $M$ leaves costs parametric or requires a documented counting/estimation procedure. More iterations need not improve success.

For static concatenated gate counts at a fixed chosen precision,
\begin{equation}
 T_{\mathrm{search}}=T_A+j(2T_A+T_{S_0}+T_O).
 \label{eq:search-cost}
\end{equation}
Synthesize $A$ once and reuse the actual emitted inverse for $A^\dagger$. A whole-algorithm budget counts $(1+2j)$ preparation occurrences and $j$ occurrences of each other component, including preprocessing errors. The planned primary operator-error budget is $10^{-3}$, with $10^{-2}$ and $10^{-4}$ sensitivity checks. These are requested tolerances, not achieved measurements. Numerical matrix admission, norm propagation, angle/precision limits, and caller allocation guards remain those of the exact reviewed compiler bytes. The count identity is neither a $T$-depth identity nor a dynamic RUS cost formula.

\section{Results: Oracle and Search Costs}
\label{sec:results-cost}
% Every number below is a row of the private claims ledger; ids are given in the comments. Tables are generated by code/make_results_tables.py.
This section reports only the cost results that have passed recount and a functional check. All counts are for the ideal regime R1 (preparation over all $2^n$ codes) with one fixed seed, the \texttt{n\_clean\_m15} lowering of multi-controlled gates, and zero arbitrary-angle rotations unless stated. They depend on a private synthesis bridge and balancer that we did not build ourselves; a locally built bridge gives identical oracle qubit, gate and depth counts in all 33 checked cases. % T4-4
The graphs are $K_3$, $K_4$ (four colors) and $C_5$ (three colors); $n$ is 6, 8 and 10 data qubits respectively. These are small instances, and none of the statements below extends to larger graphs.

\paragraph{Correctness before cost.} On $K_3$, the oracles of eight of ten methods equal $(-1)^{f(x)}$ on all 64 inputs under our own predicate; one method is too wide to simulate and one is excluded by a guard in the library. % T4-1
Gate counts below are taken only from circuits for which a per-gate hand recount agrees with the repository's Clifford+$T$ lowering. % P6, P10, P11

\input{results_tables}

\paragraph{Oracle $T$ cost (Table~\ref{tab:oracle-t}).} % P6, P10
On all three graphs the cheapest method in $T$ count is \texttt{sb-simple}, a Belletti-style hand-designed comparator variant, followed by \texttt{xag-bennett}; the structure-aware oracle is not the cheapest on any of the three. On $K_4$ and $C_5$ its $T$ count is 207 and 281 against 123 and 211 for \texttt{sb-simple}. Its $T$ depth is also higher than that of \texttt{sb-simple} on all three graphs (Table~\ref{tab:oracle-t}). The $K_3$ column omits \texttt{xag}, whose circuit contains arbitrary-angle rotations; counts with and without rotations are not comparable. % P7
\texttt{sb-original} is excluded on $K_4$ and $C_5$ by the library guard.

\paragraph{One Grover iteration (Table~\ref{tab:search-t}).} % P11, P14
For one iteration in R1 the search circuit's $T$ count equals the oracle count plus an offset that does not depend on the method: 47 for $K_4$ and 63 for $C_5$ (31 for $K_3$). Across iteration counts $j=1,2,3$ the $T$ count is exactly linear, $T_{\mathrm{search}}(j)=j\,(T_O+D)$, for the four methods tested on all three graphs. In R1 the oracle therefore decides the ranking, and preparation and diffusion do not change it. In R2/R3 preparation contains rotations whose cost depends on the chosen approximation precision, so we do not report $T$ counts for them here.

\paragraph{Logical size on $K_3$ (Table~\ref{tab:k3-qgd}).} % T4-2
Qubits, gates and depth are logical counts at mixed gate granularity and are not $T$-costed. We make no win/tie/loss or geometric-mean statement across methods: the comparison for $K_5$ and \texttt{myciel3} is backed only by the library's sampled validation and is therefore not reported. % T4-3, T4-5 pending
Our default-profile rows match the Codex line's rows in 29 of 30 cases on three graphs; the exception is $K_3$ with \texttt{aig-bennett}, which differs because we apply no preprocessing to it by default. % T4-6

\paragraph{Limits.} The three graphs have at most 10 data qubits; one seed was run; no second independent method confirms the tables beyond the hand recount; the strongest-baseline comparison on the nine frozen graphs is not complete; and no noisy or routed cost is reported.

\section{Results: Scaling, Mechanisms and Success Probability}
\label{sec:results-scaling}
% Ledger ids in comments; tables generated by code/make_scaling_tables.py from code/scaling_data.json (built by code/build_scaling_data.py from private work files).
Same conditions as Section~\ref{sec:results-cost}: regime R1, one iteration, \texttt{n\_clean\_m15} lowering, no arbitrary-angle rotations, and a private synthesis bridge and balancer that we did not build. Every count below was recomputed by a per-gate hand recount that agrees with the repository's lowering.

\paragraph{Scaling with graph size (Table~\ref{tab:fits}).} % T8-1, T8-3, T8-4
On paths and cycles with $k=3$ and $n=3$--12 vertices, the oracle $T$ count is exactly linear in $n$ for \texttt{xag} (96 $T$ per vertex), \texttt{xag-bennett} (56), \texttt{sb-simple} (44) and the structure-aware oracle (58); this was checked on 144 circuits. On 36 random graphs ($n=4$--10, $n+m\le 32$, three seeds per size) the $T$ count depends only on $(n,m)$, not on which graph: the three seeds give identical counts for every method. Exact fits are in Table~\ref{tab:fits}, where the structure-aware oracle is $-9+22n+36m$. The formulas predicted nine held-out instances exactly; the predictions were written before those circuits were built.

\paragraph{Negative result against the strongest baselines.} % T8-2, T8-5
The structure-aware oracle has the same per-vertex slope as \texttt{sb-simple} (22) but a larger per-edge slope (36) than \texttt{xag-bennett} (28) and \texttt{sb-simple} (22). It is therefore cheaper in $T$ than \texttt{xag-bennett} only when $m<0.75n-1.5$, that is on sparse, forest-like graphs, and it is never cheaper than \texttt{sb-simple} at $k=3$. On paths and cycles it is 4--12\% above \texttt{xag-bennett} and 31\% above \texttt{sb-simple} at $n=12$. Varying the number of colors on $P_6$ and $C_6$ ($k=2$--8) it beats \texttt{xag-bennett} only at $k=2$ (ratio 0.63--0.80); at $k=5,6$ it beats the best \texttt{sb-*} variant (ratios 0.62--0.75, because \texttt{sb-simple} jumps to 865--903) but not \texttt{xag-bennett} (ratios 1.03--1.27). Our hypothesis that structure-aware synthesis gives the lowest $T$ count as graphs grow is not supported against these two baselines.

\input{scaling_tables}

\paragraph{What it does win (Table~\ref{tab:p12}).} % T8-7, T8-8, T8-9
Against the Belletti-style \texttt{sb-balanced} comparator on paths and cycles up to $n=12$, the structure-aware oracle has about 25\% lower $T$ count (651 against 863 on $P_{12}$) and a $T$ depth that is lower at most sizes but tied within two layers at $P_{10}$--$P_{12}$ (177 against 175 on $P_{12}$), but it uses about 1.8 times as many qubits (70 against 39 on $P_{12}$). \texttt{sb-balanced} and \texttt{sb-minimal} grow by roughly 2.5--3 qubits per vertex, the structure-aware oracle, \texttt{xag} and \texttt{sb-simple} by 6 (\texttt{xag-bennett} is wider still: 91 on $P_{12}$). Structure-aware is deeper than \texttt{xag-bennett} and \texttt{sb-simple} at every size (177 against 135 and 93 on $P_{12}$), and on $K_5$, $K_6$ deeper than \texttt{sb-balanced} (137 against 119 and 201 against 169). The result is a trade of $T$ count against width relative to \texttt{sb-balanced}, not a dominance. $T$ depth and width were confirmed by a second script that reads the circuits and schedules $T$ layers itself.

\paragraph{Mechanisms (Tables~\ref{tab:prof-K4} and~\ref{tab:prof-C5}).} % T5-1, T5-2, T5-3
Optimization profiles lower $T$ count only through reduced multiplicative complexity, and only where the network has redundancy. On $K_4$, \texttt{none} and \texttt{refactoring} give identical $T$ counts for all five methods. On $C_5$, \texttt{refactoring} lowers \texttt{xag} from 559 to 439 and \texttt{xag-bennett} from 329 to 259 and removes five qubits, a saving of about 21\% in $T$; the 30 removed controlled-\texttt{u} gates at 4~$T$ each account for the whole drop of 120. The \texttt{balanced} profile lowers $T$ depth, not $T$ count (\texttt{xag} on $C_5$: 176 to 112 with 559 $T$ unchanged); \texttt{cut\_esop\_balancing} gives \texttt{refactoring}'s $T$ count with the depth gain. \texttt{klut-bennett} is not helped consistently and \texttt{best-fit} is unaffected. The effect depends on the graph, and with two instances we draw no aggregate conclusion beyond this: a profile ranking taken from $K_3$ and $K_4$ would mislead, and comparisons must list the profile as a factor.

\paragraph{Success probability.} % C1, X3, P13
Our ideal-statevector runs reproduce the textbook law $P_j=\sin^2((2j+1)\theta)$ with $\theta=\arcsin\sqrt{M/N}$ on $K_3$, $K_4$ and $P_4$ (R1--R3) and $C_5$ (R2, R3); ten $C_5$ R1 rows match to $10^{-10}$, and the 11 simulated cases agree to $2.5\times10^{-14}$ (the $C_5$ R1 run exceeded its time cap after four iteration counts). We also found a bug in the historical comparator path (\texttt{comparison\_circuit}): for $k=5,6$ its invalid-color check is built bit-reversed, so the success probability is far below the ideal value for every variant (e.g., $K_3$, $k=5$: 0.390 at $j=2$ against 0.969). The bug does not affect $k=3$ or powers of two, and the component-based baselines match the ideal curve to $1.3\times10^{-12}$. Success-probability comparisons against \texttt{sb-*} circuits for $k=5,6$ must therefore use the component-based path. % P9, P13

\paragraph{Limits.} Everything here is $k=3$ on paths, cycles, complete graphs up to $K_6$ and random graphs with $n+m\le 32$, except the color sweep on $P_6$ and $C_6$; one build seed. The scaling formulas are fits to a pilot family, not part of the frozen graph set, and graph independence is shown for these builders only. Counts for $n+m\ge 33$ are excluded: there \texttt{sb-simple} and the structure-aware oracle jump by a factor of 10--20 (for example 695 to 8280) because the study serializes multi-controlled gates with 33 or more controls as a phase ladder of rotations. We believe, but have not verified, that this is a serialization artifact and not method cost, so no scaling claim is made beyond $n+m=32$. Success probability was checked only with ideal statevectors; no noise or routing result is reported, and caterpillar mapping strategies and qubit-budgeted pebbling were not studied.

\section{Scope, Limitations and Validation}
\label{sec:experiments}
% Ledger ids in comments (private claims ledger). Replaces the former evaluation plan.
\textbf{What this paper establishes.} Sections~\ref{sec:results-cost} and~\ref{sec:results-scaling} report recounted Clifford+$T$ costs of oracles and one-iteration search circuits, scaling fits on paths, cycles, complete and random graphs with $k=3$, a profile study on $K_4$ and $C_5$, and ideal-statevector success probabilities. Each number is backed by a ledger row and was recomputed by a per-gate hand recount or an independent script.

\textbf{What it does not establish.}
(i)~The comparison on the nine frozen graphs against the four comparator baselines is incomplete: only $K_3$ is fully checked, and $K_5$ and \texttt{myciel3} rest on the library's sampled validation. % T4-3, T4-5
(ii)~All instances are small ($\le 10$ data qubits for the cost tables; $n+m\le 32$ for the scaling fits), with one build seed. % P10, T8-3
(iii)~Counts for $n+m\ge 33$ are excluded because the study serializes multi-controlled gates with 33 or more controls as a rotation ladder; we believe but have not verified that this is an artifact. % T8-6
(iv)~$T$ counts in regimes R2/R3 are lower bounds because preparation contains arbitrary-angle rotations that we did not price. % P12
(v)~Oracle $T$ counts depend on a private synthesis bridge and balancer built by an earlier research line; a locally built bridge reproduces the oracle sizes in the 33 cases we compared. % T4-4
(vi)~The relative-phase substitution is verified on small compositions only, and it requires a diagonal middle operation: with a non-diagonal middle it fails. % C22
(vii)~Hardware execution, physical error-correction estimates, noisy and routed costs, dynamic repeat-until-success accounting, precolored instances and conditional-workspace synthesis are outside this study. No claim is made about them.
(viii)~The historical comparator path has a bit-reversal defect in its invalid-color check for $k=5,6$; success-probability comparisons for those $k$ must use the component-based path, and we did not re-derive the published success numbers. % P9, P13

\subsection{Validation and admission boundaries}
\label{subsec:validation}
The library validates oracles exhaustively up to 12 inputs (all of $K_3$, $K_4$ and $C_5$ in Section~\ref{sec:results-cost}) and by seeded sampling above that, where sampled coverage is not a proof; % P10, T8-3
 functional equality with $(-1)^{f(x)}$ was verified by statevector on $K_3$. % T4-1, T4-2
Ideal multi-iteration runs were executed only within a 22-qubit statevector cap, so larger instances are analytical only. % C12, C1
The relative-phase Toffoli substitution was checked on full unitaries of small oracles. % C22

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
The construction distinguishes valid codes from proper colorings, restores oracle workspace, and matches diffusion to preparation. In the instances we recounted, the structure-aware oracle is not the cheapest in $T$ count against the strongest synthesis and comparator baselines: it is cheaper than \texttt{xag-bennett} only on sparse graphs and at $k=2$, and never cheaper than \texttt{sb-simple} at $k=3$. Against the Belletti-style \texttt{sb-balanced} comparator it saves about 25\% in $T$ count on paths and cycles, at about 1.8 times the qubits. The $T$ count of one-iteration search in R1 is the oracle count plus a method-independent offset, and ideal success probabilities follow the textbook law. These are findings for small $k=3$ instances; they are not evidence of scalability, noisy performance or advantage on the full benchmark set, and the open items listed in Section~\ref{sec:experiments} remain.
